book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook lists PLR, BPLR, base rate and MCLR with definitions and dates. The video starts with the problem as a lived scene (a customer haggling a loan rate down like vegetables at a cart), names the system only after the scene, then tells each later system as a repair of the previous one's failure: each rule is introduced with its goal, tested (a 2010 report, staged as a second role-play between RBI and the banks), shown failing, and replaced. The cause of failure (banks competing for customers) was already planted in the opening scene by the rival bank's lower offer.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each system is one piece told as problem -> rule -> goal -> test -> failure or success, with the failure of one system becoming the reason for the next.

opening.what: 'You will be surprised': in the 1970s loan interest was haggled like buying vegetables from a cart; a bank clerk welcomes a customer and the role-play begins.

moves.concept: PLR system: each bank sets its own benchmark

moves.concept: BPLR as RBI's floor and its two goals

examples.what: A customer haggles a 10 lakh loan: the bank's 15% falls to 12%, then 7% as the loan grows to 20 lakh, then 5% when she threatens to go to the bank across the road offering 6%.
examples.carries: rates set by bargaining under PLR, and competition between banks as the force pushing rates down (reused later as the reason BPLR failed)

examples.what: Loan interest haggled like vegetables bought from a cart.
One bank, four identical borrowers paying 5%, 15%, 12% and 3% (on screen).
A creditworthy customer pictured as someone who borrowed before and always repaid on time.
examples.carries: why the best customer gets the lowest rate, so BPLR looks like a minimum

examples.what: RBI as a stern elder checking on banks; banks answer 'look, big father, the minimum was your assumption'.
examples.carries: why BPLR failed: it was never a binding floor and competition pushed rates below it

examples.what: A 2010 report: 77% of all bank lending below BPLR (as stated).
examples.carries: the evidence that the floor failed

examples.what: If operating expenses go into the calculation and differ by bank, base rates must differ by bank.
examples.carries: why each bank's base rate is different yet still a floor

closing.what: Base rate declared a success, then a 2015 'mess' is teased as the reason for MCLR, with a playlist plug; no recap of the three systems.

narration.density: About 14 terms (PLR, benchmark rate, cost of funds, transparency, standardisation, BPLR, creditworthy customer, credit history, regulate, base rate, deregulated, operating expenses, CRR cost on screen, MCLR) in about 7 minutes, about 2 per minute. Comfortable: two role-plays take about 2 of the 7 minutes and carry the reasoning, so the pace suits a first look; the BPLR definition stretch (115-179) is the densest and least clear.

talmel_summary: In the role-play and the BPLR set-up the picture shows the step at the moment of the words: struck rate tags climb as the bargain moves, four identical borrowers wear different tags, the phrase 'most creditworthy customer' turns into a person, and later one bank gets a gold ring while the RBI arrows flip direction. Where the argument gets abstract (the 77% finding, the banks' reason, the base-rate inputs) the screen switches to text lines that appear several seconds before the voice or add parts the voice never says. The best device is planting the two goals (transparency, standardisation) as chips that are later crossed and then ticked on the same objects.

voice.notes: About 177 words per minute. The opening role-play uses two distinct character voices (a smooth clerk, a firm woman customer addressed as 'devi ji') with natural haggling rhythm: offer, refusal, counter-offer, threat, panic ('arre nahi nahi, ruko ruko'). The narrator is conversational and uses idioms for institutions ('hawa tight', 'bade baapa', 'chain ki saans li'), which makes RBI and the banks feel like characters. Numbers are read plainly ('10 lakh', '15%', '77%'); years in full. Key conclusions are marked with 'to ab yahan par yeh baat saaf ho gayi hai'. Ends on a question-style teaser for MCLR.

game_ideas.player_does: Plays the borrower at a 1970s bank counter: asks for a lower rate, raises the loan amount, or points to the rival bank's offer.
game_ideas.process_happens: The clerk's rate tag is struck and rewritten lower with each move, keeping the ladder visible; then three other borrowers of the same bank appear with their own bargained rates.
game_ideas.win: Get a low rate, then see the side-by-side tags and correctly light the two missing chips: no transparency, no standardisation.
game_ideas.lose: Accepting the first offer leaves the learner at 15% while a neighbour pays 3% for the same loan, which is exactly the PLR problem.
game_ideas.concept: bargained rates under PLR and why they lacked transparency and standardisation

game_ideas.player_does: Plays RBI: picks the rule (PLR: banks free; BPLR: rate for the best customer taken as the minimum; base rate: each bank's cost-based floor, below which lending is barred) and runs a year of lending by four competing banks.
game_ideas.process_happens: 100 loan tokens fall from the four banks onto a floor line; under BPLR competition pushes most of them below the line (about 77 of 100), under base rate none can cross it; the transparency and standardisation chips get a cross or a tick.
game_ideas.win: End a year with no loans below the floor and both chips ticked (only the base-rate rule does this).
game_ideas.lose: Choosing BPLR shows the tokens sliding under the floor and the banks' speech bubble 'minimum was your assumption'.
game_ideas.concept: why BPLR failed and the base rate held

game_ideas.player_does: Builds a bank's base rate by stacking blocks: cost of funds, operating expenses, minimum return, cost of keeping CRR (mechanic: build a rate from its parts).
game_ideas.process_happens: The stack's height becomes that bank's floor line; a second bank with higher operating expenses builds a taller stack; customers' requested rates below the line are refused.
game_ideas.win: Set two banks' floors correctly and explain why they differ.
game_ideas.lose: Leaving out operating expenses makes the floor too low and the bank lends at a loss, shown as a red cost bar sticking out above the rate.
game_ideas.concept: base rate calculation and why base rates differ by bank

game_ideas.player_does: Places cards on the era strip: bargained PLR (1973), BPLR (2003), 2010 report with 77% below BPLR, base rate (2010), new trouble and MCLR (2015).
game_ideas.process_happens: Each card drops a heading from its tick with the dotted line, as in the video, and the goal chips change from crossed to ticked at the base rate.
game_ideas.win: Strip complete with each system's failure leading to the next.
game_ideas.lose: Placing base rate before the 2010 report shows no reason yet for a new system and nudges the learner to place the evidence first.

checks_learned: In a role-play opening, the term is named only after the scene ends, and the later explanation of failure must point back to a moment of the scene (here the rival-bank offer becomes the competition reason).
When a number in a running example is revised, the old value stays visible and struck, so the history of the change can be read.
Every item of an on-screen list must be spoken (three of the four base-rate inputs are never said).
A text answer must not appear more than about 3 s before the voice gives it (the 'because banks were competing' line leads by about 6 s).
Key evidence numbers (77% of lending below the floor) must be drawn as a quantity against the floor line, not only written.
Goals planted as on-screen chips must be resolved on the same chips (cross on failure, tick on success); E25 does this well.
Statements about who decides (RBI fixed BPLR vs BPLR settled with banks) must stay consistent within one lesson; flag contradictions between narration lines.
When two successive systems are compared, reuse one scene and change only the parts that differ (tag, ring, arrow direction).

teaching_best.why: The role-play makes the problem felt before any term: the struck rate ladder and the rival-bank threat carry both 'rates were bargained' and 'competition pushes rates down'.
One bank and four identical people with different rate tags makes 'no standardisation' visible without reading.
The learner's obvious objection is put in RBI's mouth and answered by the banks, exposing that the 'minimum' was only an assumption.
The BPLR picture is reused for base rate; a gold ring on one bank and flipped arrows show that authority moved from RBI to each bank.
'Observe' cause chain: operating expenses differ by bank, so base rates must differ, yet each is a floor.

teaching_weak.why: BPLR is defined by a paragraph before any picture, and the chain best customer -> lowest rate -> floor is spoken fast in one long sentence.
The 77% finding and its reason are text lines; the main evidence of the video is never drawn.
The base-rate calculation is a four-item list and only one item is spoken.
The narration says RBI fixed BPLR, while the role-play says BPLR was settled with the banks; the learner gets two stories of who decided.
Ends on a teaser without recapping the three systems side by side.
